papers.title: What Differs Between the Twins Is Not a Lagging Clock but the Length of a Worldline ── Time Dilation Read Through the Yamagishi Zero-Tension: the Null Hypothesis of Instrumental Lag Is Rejected by the Muon ── [Paper 123]
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: What Differs Between the Twins Is Not a Lagging Clock but the Length of a Worldline: time dilation read through the Yamagishi zero-tension, and the null hypothesis of instrumental lag rejected by the muon. The popular line that a moving clock runs slow invites a natural question in whoever hears it: slow relative to what, and is the clock not simply going wrong? This paper states that question as a falsifiable null hypothesis (Paper 89), writes down which data reject it, and then shows that what invited the question was not the physics but the sentence. THIS IS NOT A PAPER THAT DOUBTS RELATIVITY. Time dilation is real, and this paper marshals the data supporting it. NO NEW PHYSICAL LAW AND NO NEW THEOREM. Null hypothesis H0: time dilation is an instrumental lag. A moving clock's mechanism is dulled so that its reading falls behind, and the reading regains its correctness once the clock is at rest. H0 is not empty: it has three testable consequences — (a) different mechanisms would lag differently, (b) what is not a clock would not lag, (c) the difference would vanish at rest. For all three the experiment exists. Rejection (b): a muon is not a clock. Bailey et al. (1977, Nature 268, 301) measured the lifetime of muons at gamma = 29.33 in a storage ring. Against a rest lifetime of 2.1948 plus or minus 0.0010 microseconds, the lifetimes in flight were 64.419 plus or minus 0.058 and 64.368 plus or minus 0.029 microseconds for positive and negative muons. Special relativity predicts 64.373 microseconds, differing from the measurement by 0.71 parts in a thousand (recomputed here; the paper's own figure is that the time transformation holds to 0.8 plus or minus 0.7 parts in a thousand). A muon contains no oscillator, no spring, no gears — there is no mechanism in it that could lag. Yet its decay ran slower by exactly gamma. With no instrument to lag, instrumental lag cannot account for the fact. The size of the effect is dramatic too: c times the rest lifetime is 658.6 metres, so without dilation the fraction of muons surviving 15 kilometres of atmosphere would be 1.29 times ten to the minus ten; at gamma = 20 the decay length becomes 13156 metres and the survival fraction 0.32, a factor of 2.5 billion (computed here). That muons are observed at ground level is itself a direct consequence of time dilation. Rejection (a): the mechanism is irrelevant. Time dilation has been confirmed with instruments sharing no principle of operation — caesium clocks (a hyperfine transition), hydrogen masers (a different atom and transition), optical lattice clocks (an optical transition orders of magnitude away), spectral lines (not a clock at all), and muon decay (no oscillator). If the slowing were a dulling of a mechanism, unlike mechanisms would be dulled by unlike amounts; they are dulled by the same amount. What these share is not a mechanism but a worldline, which means the agreement is on the worldline's side. Rejection (c): the difference survives the return to rest. Hafele and Keating (1971) flew caesium clocks twice around the world, eastward and westward, and compared them at rest with the clocks of the U.S. Naval Observatory on their return. Eastward the prediction was minus 40 plus or minus 23 nanoseconds and the observation minus 59 plus or minus 10; westward the prediction was plus 275 plus or minus 21 and the observation plus 273 plus or minus 7. The difference was not recovered. A lag would correct itself once the motion ceased; this did not. What remains is not a wrong reading but a difference in the time that elapsed. There is also a refuting apparatus in continuous operation: for a GPS satellite (orbital radius 2.656 times ten to the seventh metres, speed 3874 metres per second) special relativity gives minus 7.2 microseconds per day and general relativity plus 45.9, a net plus 38.6 (computed here from the orbital elements). Uncorrected, the ranging error grows by 11.6 kilometres per day, and this correction has been applied daily for decades. So what invited the question? This is the second core of the paper. The word slow tacitly posits something to be slow relative to, and no universal clock exists. The most that can be posited is another observer's coordinate time, and from that observer's side the first clock is slow in return. So the question which one is really slower has no answer, and what makes people ask an unanswerable question is the form of the sentence. The one who asked did not err — the sentence invited an ill-formed question. This is the category error diagnosed in Paper 118: the coordinate dt is a label pinned to the manifold while proper time dtau is a functional of a curve, and saying the clock runs slow treats dtau as though it were dt, speaking of a quantity that may differ from curve to curve as if it were a scale everyone shares. Popular expositions keep reproducing the confusion not because the physics is unsettled but because they keep using a sentence with the categories crossed. Put correctly, the question does not arise. Since Minkowski (1908; Paper 108) the correct statement has been that dtau squared equals dt squared minus the spatial part over c squared, and that proper time is the integral of dtau along the worldline. Proper time is the length of a worldline. The two twins joined the same two events by two different paths; the paths differ in length, and that is all. Neither clock went wrong — each measured the length of its own worldline correctly and in full. What differs is what was measured, not the instrument that measured it. For ten years of coordinate time the proper time is 8.66 years at v/c = 0.5, 6.00 at 0.8, 4.36 at 0.9, 1.41 at 0.99, and 0.10 at 0.99995 (computed here). The same restatement answers the objection that motion is relative and the situation should be symmetric: it is not symmetric, because only one twin changes inertial frame, and this is not a matter of description — give each twin an accelerometer and the readings differ. In geometric terms the traveller's worldline is bent and the stay-at-home's is straight, and in Minkowski geometry the straight path maximises proper time, the opposite of Euclidean geometry where the straight path is shortest. The bent path is shorter; that is the whole of it. An honest brake. The processes confirmed to follow time dilation are many: the caesium hyperfine transition, the hydrogen maser, optical lattice transitions, atomic spectral lines, and muon decay. None is known to disobey. But no human has been carried at relativistic speed; the Hafele-Keating aircraft were subsonic and the differences there were of order a tenth of a microsecond. The statement that a person would not age is an induction over processes. The induction is very strong — a living body is made of chemical reactions, chemical reactions are electromagnetic, and that electromagnetic processes follow proper time has been confirmed repeatedly since Ives-Stilwell; to posit a physical process that does not follow proper time is to discard known physics. Even so, an induction is not an observation. What is established is that every process tested follows proper time; that a person would not age is one step beyond that. Not writing that step with the force of an observation is also the honest reply to whoever raised the question. The phrase the Urashima effect bundles two claims — that the proper time is shorter (established, treated here) and that it felt shorter to the traveller (not treated here, outside physics). The latter is the quantity Paper 118 explicitly refused to enter into the physics census, and it is quarantined here as Layer 3. IMPORTANT (scope): an organisation of established standard facts and a diagnosis of a popular phrasing (Layer 2). Every experiment used is established (Bailey et al. 1977, Hafele-Keating 1971, Ives-Stilwell 1938, Vessot et al. 1980, GPS). NO NEW THEOREM AND NO PREDICTION. What is not claimed: any new physical law (there is none) / any doubt about relativity (this paper is on the side of time dilation) / an observation that a person would not age (that is an induction over processes) / anything about felt time (outside the physics census, quarantined as Layer 3) / that acceleration is the cause (acceleration breaks the symmetry, but what gives the difference in proper time is the shape of the worldline). What remains: when a question keeps arising, suspect the sentence before the physics. On the making of this work: The ideas and content of this work stem from the author's own considerations. Assistance from an AI (a large language model) was used for structuring, English translation, and checking the algebra. Any remaining errors or misinterpretations are solely the author's. papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Financial Decision-Making: Opportunities, Challenges and Implications for the Modern Financial Sector
papers.venue: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is quickly taking center stage in modern financial decision-making. The capacity of financial institutions and investors to analyze vast and intricate data sets has increased thanks to developments in machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, predictive analytics, and generative artificial intelligence. Conventional methods for investment analysis, credit evaluation, fraud detection, financial forecasting, risk assessment, and portfolio management have been altered by the growing use of AI. This study looks at the expanding use of AI in financial decision-making and assesses both its possible advantages and the difficulties in implementing it. While taking into account issues with data quality, algorithmic bias, privacy, cybersecurity, explainability, model risk, and an over-reliance on automated systems, the study focuses on how AI can enhance the speed, consistency, analytical depth, and efficiency of financial decisions. Using contemporary scholarly and institutional literature on AI and finance, a descriptive and analytical research technique is used. According to the investigation, AI may greatly improve financial decision-support by digesting data quickly and seeing connections that conventional analytical techniques can miss. However, data quality, model architecture, governance, and human oversight all have a significant impact on how successful AI is. Increasing the use of AI can potentially lead to new vulnerabilities in the financial industry, especially through third-party concentration, cyber risks, market correlations, and model risk, according to recent international data. The study comes to the conclusion that rather than completely replacing human judgment, AI should be included into finance largely as an enhancement of human competence. Strong governance, open decision-making procedures, trustworthy data, ongoing model review, and significant human monitoring are all necessary for responsible deployment. The study offers a theoretical framework for comprehending how financial institutions might profit from AI while managing the dangers related to technology, ethics, and finances.

papers.title: The Free-Energy Architecture of Discovery-Capable Intelligence
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Large language models optimise fluently inside a fixed representational space but do not reliably produce genuine discovery; the field has treated this as a tuning problem. We argue it is an architectural one, and we derive the required architecture from first principles rather than inferring it from current systems. The derivation rests on a single, established formalism used in its exact form: variational free energy, F = complexity − accuracy, which is simultaneously a thermodynamic quantity (U − TS) and a statement about how well an internal generative model fits the world under an Occam penalty. Read this way, intelligence is the minimisation of free energy: the pruning of the space of conceivable representations by the joint constraint of logic (the prior) and the physical world (the likelihood), with perception and action as the two variables that lower the same scalar. We discipline the claim with the Landauer test — the standard by which "information" earns causal status only when an abstract property forces a substrate-independent physical consequence — and we bound it with highly optimised tolerance (the conservation of vulnerability): an optimised system cannot abolish fragility, only relocate it to the edge of what its model covers, so a discovery-capable architecture must make that boundary explicit rather than fail at it silently. A note on rigor and terminology. The paper's physical claims are not rhetorical flourish, and they are not softened into mere analogy: each is held to the Landauer test of §2, which admits an abstract, information-theoretic quantity as physically causal only when it forces a substrate-independent physical consequence. Where a claim meets that bar we state it as physics; where itdoes not, we flag it as correctly applied statistical mechanics of a representational system, not a new physics of information. Entropy is used throughout in its standard sense — representational disorder, measured where stated. This theory makes four architectural demands, and we discharge each against an auditable engine, SEMPL, a constrained-natural-language process engine whose generative model is declared — which lets us demonstrate the free-energy principle in its falsifiable form, a claim neither the neuroscience nor the LLM literature can cleanly make. We give: (i) a single free-energy objective over the engine's repair operation that reproduces, rather than replaces, the programme's prior measured results — the deterministic collapse of a permuted process's ordering entropy to zero becomes an accuracy term driven to zero, and the reduction of a domain's declared structure to its minimal load-bearing residue becomes a complexity-term delta; (ii) program-structural self-maintenance, in which the engine models its own source and surfaces a real module-dependency cycle and a real generality gap in its own ordering machinery; (iii) composable discovery methods that construct process structure (the action face of active inference), bounded and bridge-free; and (iv) a coverage-frontier instrument that flags out-of-model inputs as boundary conditions rather than returning them as confident answers. Around these sits a governed discovery loop — inject → generate → verify → repair → adopt — whose defining property is a machine-checked, byte-identical verify-before-adopt gate; it is the reproducible, formal complement to expert-in-the-loop frontier generators. We then prove the architecture at domain scale. We model a mid-size company's accounting function as ten inter-referable workflow processes sharing a general-ledger backbone; all ten repair to bridge-free free-energy fixpoints, and the family is a genuine network rather than isolated demonstrations. On it we perform the capstone discovery: finding a missing internal control by cross-process analogy — the engine identifies that one payment process discloses money with no independent approval, unlike its siblings, names the exact missing control, verifies in a sandbox that inserting it closes the gap bridge-free, and proposes it for human approval. This is a real audit finding and the concrete embodiment of the conservation-of-vulnerability thesis: the discovered gap is precisely the fragility displaced to where the control is absent. Beyond the demonstration, the architecture speaks directly to the enterprise agentic-AI question: a governed, inter-operable semantic substrate that ingests LLM-generated process representations turns a fleet of task-executing agents into a single auditable, self-maintaining, and self-auditing workflow — with simplification, efficiency, and controlled long-term evolution following from the theory rather than from ad-hoc engineering (nothing is more practical than a good theory). Every result is deterministic and reproducible, and is established with full reproduction artifacts in the companionworking papers rather than in this synthesis. We are explicit about what is not claimed: the verification is machine-checked but confined to a bounded formal representation, not frontier reach; the free-energy account is falsifiable here only because the model is declared; and live-generator quality evaluation is deferred. The contribution is a complete line from a physical principle of intelligence, through the architecture it necessitates, to a working, governed, reproducible proof that the architecture discovers something real.

papers.title: What Differs Between the Twins Is Not a Lagging Clock but the Length of a Worldline ── Time Dilation Read Through the Yamagishi Zero-Tension: the Null Hypothesis of Instrumental Lag Is Rejected by the Muon ── [Paper 123]
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: What Differs Between the Twins Is Not a Lagging Clock but the Length of a Worldline: time dilation read through the Yamagishi zero-tension, and the null hypothesis of instrumental lag rejected by the muon. The popular line that a moving clock runs slow invites a natural question in whoever hears it: slow relative to what, and is the clock not simply going wrong? This paper states that question as a falsifiable null hypothesis (Paper 89), writes down which data reject it, and then shows that what invited the question was not the physics but the sentence. THIS IS NOT A PAPER THAT DOUBTS RELATIVITY. Time dilation is real, and this paper marshals the data supporting it. NO NEW PHYSICAL LAW AND NO NEW THEOREM. Null hypothesis H0: time dilation is an instrumental lag. A moving clock's mechanism is dulled so that its reading falls behind, and the reading regains its correctness once the clock is at rest. H0 is not empty: it has three testable consequences — (a) different mechanisms would lag differently, (b) what is not a clock would not lag, (c) the difference would vanish at rest. For all three the experiment exists. Rejection (b): a muon is not a clock. Bailey et al. (1977, Nature 268, 301) measured the lifetime of muons at gamma = 29.33 in a storage ring. Against a rest lifetime of 2.1948 plus or minus 0.0010 microseconds, the lifetimes in flight were 64.419 plus or minus 0.058 and 64.368 plus or minus 0.029 microseconds for positive and negative muons. Special relativity predicts 64.373 microseconds, differing from the measurement by 0.71 parts in a thousand (recomputed here; the paper's own figure is that the time transformation holds to 0.8 plus or minus 0.7 parts in a thousand). A muon contains no oscillator, no spring, no gears — there is no mechanism in it that could lag. Yet its decay ran slower by exactly gamma. With no instrument to lag, instrumental lag cannot account for the fact. The size of the effect is dramatic too: c times the rest lifetime is 658.6 metres, so without dilation the fraction of muons surviving 15 kilometres of atmosphere would be 1.29 times ten to the minus ten; at gamma = 20 the decay length becomes 13156 metres and the survival fraction 0.32, a factor of 2.5 billion (computed here). That muons are observed at ground level is itself a direct consequence of time dilation. Rejection (a): the mechanism is irrelevant. Time dilation has been confirmed with instruments sharing no principle of operation — caesium clocks (a hyperfine transition), hydrogen masers (a different atom and transition), optical lattice clocks (an optical transition orders of magnitude away), spectral lines (not a clock at all), and muon decay (no oscillator). If the slowing were a dulling of a mechanism, unlike mechanisms would be dulled by unlike amounts; they are dulled by the same amount. What these share is not a mechanism but a worldline, which means the agreement is on the worldline's side. Rejection (c): the difference survives the return to rest. Hafele and Keating (1971) flew caesium clocks twice around the world, eastward and westward, and compared them at rest with the clocks of the U.S. Naval Observatory on their return. Eastward the prediction was minus 40 plus or minus 23 nanoseconds and the observation minus 59 plus or minus 10; westward the prediction was plus 275 plus or minus 21 and the observation plus 273 plus or minus 7. The difference was not recovered. A lag would correct itself once the motion ceased; this did not. What remains is not a wrong reading but a difference in the time that elapsed. There is also a refuting apparatus in continuous operation: for a GPS satellite (orbital radius 2.656 times ten to the seventh metres, speed 3874 metres per second) special relativity gives minus 7.2 microseconds per day and general relativity plus 45.9, a net plus 38.6 (computed here from the orbital elements). Uncorrected, the ranging error grows by 11.6 kilometres per day, and this correction has been applied daily for decades. So what invited the question? This is the second core of the paper. The word slow tacitly posits something to be slow relative to, and no universal clock exists. The most that can be posited is another observer's coordinate time, and from that observer's side the first clock is slow in return. So the question which one is really slower has no answer, and what makes people ask an unanswerable question is the form of the sentence. The one who asked did not err — the sentence invited an ill-formed question. This is the category error diagnosed in Paper 118: the coordinate dt is a label pinned to the manifold while proper time dtau is a functional of a curve, and saying the clock runs slow treats dtau as though it were dt, speaking of a quantity that may differ from curve to curve as if it were a scale everyone shares. Popular expositions keep reproducing the confusion not because the physics is unsettled but because they keep using a sentence with the categories crossed. Put correctly, the question does not arise. Since Minkowski (1908; Paper 108) the correct statement has been that dtau squared equals dt squared minus the spatial part over c squared, and that proper time is the integral of dtau along the worldline. Proper time is the length of a worldline. The two twins joined the same two events by two different paths; the paths differ in length, and that is all. Neither clock went wrong — each measured the length of its own worldline correctly and in full. What differs is what was measured, not the instrument that measured it. For ten years of coordinate time the proper time is 8.66 years at v/c = 0.5, 6.00 at 0.8, 4.36 at 0.9, 1.41 at 0.99, and 0.10 at 0.99995 (computed here). The same restatement answers the objection that motion is relative and the situation should be symmetric: it is not symmetric, because only one twin changes inertial frame, and this is not a matter of description — give each twin an accelerometer and the readings differ. In geometric terms the traveller's worldline is bent and the stay-at-home's is straight, and in Minkowski geometry the straight path maximises proper time, the opposite of Euclidean geometry where the straight path is shortest. The bent path is shorter; that is the whole of it. An honest brake. The processes confirmed to follow time dilation are many: the caesium hyperfine transition, the hydrogen maser, optical lattice transitions, atomic spectral lines, and muon decay. None is known to disobey. But no human has been carried at relativistic speed; the Hafele-Keating aircraft were subsonic and the differences there were of order a tenth of a microsecond. The statement that a person would not age is an induction over processes. The induction is very strong — a living body is made of chemical reactions, chemical reactions are electromagnetic, and that electromagnetic processes follow proper time has been confirmed repeatedly since Ives-Stilwell; to posit a physical process that does not follow proper time is to discard known physics. Even so, an induction is not an observation. What is established is that every process tested follows proper time; that a person would not age is one step beyond that. Not writing that step with the force of an observation is also the honest reply to whoever raised the question. The phrase the Urashima effect bundles two claims — that the proper time is shorter (established, treated here) and that it felt shorter to the traveller (not treated here, outside physics). The latter is the quantity Paper 118 explicitly refused to enter into the physics census, and it is quarantined here as Layer 3. IMPORTANT (scope): an organisation of established standard facts and a diagnosis of a popular phrasing (Layer 2). Every experiment used is established (Bailey et al. 1977, Hafele-Keating 1971, Ives-Stilwell 1938, Vessot et al. 1980, GPS). NO NEW THEOREM AND NO PREDICTION. What is not claimed: any new physical law (there is none) / any doubt about relativity (this paper is on the side of time dilation) / an observation that a person would not age (that is an induction over processes) / anything about felt time (outside the physics census, quarantined as Layer 3) / that acceleration is the cause (acceleration breaks the symmetry, but what gives the difference in proper time is the shape of the worldline). What remains: when a question keeps arising, suspect the sentence before the physics. On the making of this work: The ideas and content of this work stem from the author's own considerations. Assistance from an AI (a large language model) was used for structuring, English translation, and checking the algebra. Any remaining errors or misinterpretations are solely the author's. Feedback and corrections are sincerely appreciated. ----- 双子が違うのは時計の遅れではなく、世界線の長さである——山岸ゼロテンションで読む時間の遅れ:装置の遅延という帰無仮説はミューオンが棄却する。 「動いている時計は遅れる」という通俗の一行は、聞いた者に自然な疑問を招く——何に対して遅いのか、それは時計が狂っているだけではないのか。本稿はこの疑問を破れうる帰無仮説として立て(論文89)、どのデータがそれを棄却するかを書き、そのうえで疑問を招いたのは物理ではなく言い方であることを示す。本稿は相対性理論を疑う論文ではない。時間の遅れは実在し、本稿はそれを支持するデータを整理する。新しい物理法則も新しい定理もない。 帰無仮説 H0:時間の遅れは装置の遅延である。すなわち動く時計はその機構が鈍って表示が遅れ、静止に戻れば表示は正しさを取り戻す。この H0 は空虚ではなく、三つの検査可能な帰結を持つ——(a) 機構ごとに遅れ方が違うはず、(b) 時計でないものは遅れないはず、(c) 静止に戻れば差は消えるはず。三つとも実験が存在する。 棄却(b):ミューオンは時計ではない。Bailey ら(1977、Nature 268, 301)は蓄積リング中の γ=29.33 のミューオンの寿命を測った。静止時の固有寿命 2.1948±0.0010 μs に対し、飛行中は τ+ = 64.419±0.058 μs、τ− = 64.368±0.029 μs。特殊相対論の予言 γτ0 = 64.373 μs との差は 0.71×10⁻³ である(本稿で再計算。論文自身の評価では時間変換は (0.8±0.7)×10⁻³ の精度で成立)。ミューオンには振動子もばねも歯車も入っていない——遅れうる機構が存在しない。それでもその崩壊がちょうど γ 倍だけ遅くなった。遅れる装置が無いのだから、「装置の遅延」ではこの事実を説明できない。効果の大きさも劇的である:cτ0 = 658.6 m なので、時間の遅れが無ければ大気 15 km を生き延びる割合は 1.29×10⁻¹⁰ にすぎないが、γ=20 では崩壊長が 13156 m へ伸び生存率は 0.32——2.5×10⁹ 倍である(本稿で計算)。地表でミューオンが観測されること自体が、時間の遅れの直接の帰結である。 棄却(a):機構は無関係である。時間の遅れは、互いに原理を共有しない測定器で確認されている——セシウム原子時計(超微細遷移)、水素メーザー(別の原子の別の遷移)、光格子時計(けた違いの周波数の光学遷移)、スペクトル線(そもそも時計ではない)、ミューオン崩壊(振動子が無い)。もし遅れが機構の鈍化ならば機構ごとに違う量だけ鈍るはずだが、実際には同じ量である。これらが共有しているのは機構ではなく世界線だけであり、一致しているのは世界線の側の量であることを意味する。 棄却(c):

papers.title: NeuroShield IDS: AI-Powered Intrusion and Scam Detection System
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract Network intrusions and phishing attacks are growing problems for digital infrastructure. Spam messages and fraudulent legal notices add to the threat. Most Intrusion Detection Systems and spam filters still work separately, though. They also rely on static, rule-based logic. That does not hold up well against adaptive adversaries and new attack patterns. This paper presents NeuroShield IDS, an AI-powered system. It brings network intrusion detection and NLP-based scam/phishing classification into one place. Random Forest handles network-threat classification on the NSL-KDD and CICIDS2017 datasets. Naive Bayes with TF IDF vectorization handles scam and phishing detection on the SMS Spam Collection Dataset. A unified risk-scoring engine combines the severity signals from both modules. It sends real-time alerts through a Flask/Streamlit dashboard. Our experiments show over 97% accuracy for network intrusion detection. Scam classification stays above 95%. F1-scores hold up strong across every threat category. Keywords—Intrusion Detection System (IDS); Machine Learning; Random Forest; Naive Bayes; TF-IDF; Natural Language Processing (NLP); Phishing Detection; Cybersecurity; NSL-KDD; CICIDS2017; Risk Scoring

papers.title: Role of Artificial Intelligence in Cancer Research Education
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
papers.abstract: Cancer remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide, driving urgent demand for advanced research and education frameworks capable of keeping pace with rapidly evolving scientific knowledge. Traditional cancer research education has increasingly demonstrated its limitations in preparing future researchers to handle the computational complexity of modern oncological data. Artificial intelligence (AI), encompassing machine learning, deep learning, and natural language processing, has emerged as a transformative force in both cancer research and biomedical education. This paper examines the multifaceted role of AI in cancer research education, exploring its applications in diagnostic training, genomic data interpretation, drug discovery pedagogy, and simulation-based learning environments. Despite documented benefits including enhanced diagnostic accuracy, accelerated competency development, and improved clinical reasoning a critical research gap persists: the absence of structured, oncology-specific AI curriculum frameworks with measurable educational outcomes. Current integration remains fragmented, with most programmes lacking standardised competency benchmarks and empirical evaluation. Key challenges include algorithmic bias, data privacy constraints, high computational costs, and insufficient interdisciplinary faculty expertise. This review synthesises evidence from peer-reviewed literature published between 2020 and 2025 to propose a forward-looking agenda for AI-integrated cancer research education. Future directions emphasise adaptive learning platforms, hybrid pedagogical models, and interdisciplinary training pathways as essential strategies for closing the gap between AI's clinical promise and its educational reality.

papers.title: AntEngage Empathy Conversation Dataset
papers.venue: CDI B2Share
papers.abstract: AntEngage Empathy Conversation Dataset (Version 1.0.0) is an open-access dataset containing 4,008 AI-synthesized multi-turn empathy-focused conversations designed for research and development in natural language processing, conversational AI, and affective computing. The dataset was created by AntEngage Technology Private Limited as part of the AntEngage Language Model (AELM) initiative. Each conversation represents realistic emotional support interactions involving situations such as caregiver burnout, grief, loneliness, workplace stress, parenting challenges, and emotional exhaustion. Dialogues were generated using a structured synthetic data generation pipeline followed by automated quality verification to improve diversity, coherence, naturalness, and safety. No conversations were collected from real individuals. The dataset contains no personally identifiable information (PII) and consists entirely of AI-generated content intended for research and model development. The primary objective of this dataset is to support the development and evaluation of empathetic dialogue systems, conversational agents, instruction tuning datasets, and language models capable of producing supportive and emotionally appropriate responses. Although the conversations model supportive communication, they are not a substitute for professional medical or mental health advice. Dataset Original : AntEngage Open Datasets

papers.title: Role of Artificial Intelligence in Cancer Research Education
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
papers.abstract: Cancer remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide, driving urgent demand for advanced research and education frameworks capable of keeping pace with rapidly evolving scientific knowledge. Traditional cancer research education has increasingly demonstrated its limitations in preparing future researchers to handle the computational complexity of modern oncological data. Artificial intelligence (AI), encompassing machine learning, deep learning, and natural language processing, has emerged as a transformative force in both cancer research and biomedical education. This paper examines the multifaceted role of AI in cancer research education, exploring its applications in diagnostic training, genomic data interpretation, drug discovery pedagogy, and simulation-based learning environments. Despite documented benefits including enhanced diagnostic accuracy, accelerated competency development, and improved clinical reasoning a critical research gap persists: the absence of structured, oncology-specific AI curriculum frameworks with measurable educational outcomes. Current integration remains fragmented, with most programmes lacking standardised competency benchmarks and empirical evaluation. Key challenges include algorithmic bias, data privacy constraints, high computational costs, and insufficient interdisciplinary faculty expertise. This review synthesises evidence from peer-reviewed literature published between 2020 and 2025 to propose a forward-looking agenda for AI-integrated cancer research education. Future directions emphasise adaptive learning platforms, hybrid pedagogical models, and interdisciplinary training pathways as essential strategies for closing the gap between AI's clinical promise and its educational reality.

papers.title: Quantifying Meaning: A Review of Semantic Information Analysis, Uncertainties, and Possibilistic Restrictions in Hybrid Systems
papers.venue: International Journal of Mathematics Trends and Technology
papers.abstract: Classical information theory, originating with Shannon’s foundational work [1], treats information as a purely syntactic quantity divorced from meaning. Intelligent systems operating in real-world environments must nonetheless process semantic content carried in natural language — content permeated by vagueness, fuzziness, ambiguity, and multimodal uncertainty. This article presents a structured review of the conceptual and mathematical landscape surrounding semantic information theory, proceeding from Shannon’s technical framework through Weaver’s three-level communication model, Floridi’s strongly semantic theory, Zadeh’s restriction-centred view of natural language, and contemporary rate-distortion-based semantic communication theory, toward a possibilistic approach suited to modern human-machine hybrid systems. The review is organised along four axes: (i) a rigorous taxonomy of uncertainty types along the dimensions of nature, object, and severity; (ii) a hierarchy of Levels Of Abstraction (LOA) linking raw sensor data to high-level semantic content; (iii) a critical, comparative appraisal of classical and contemporary methodologies, including the Bar-Hillel–Carnap paradox, Floridi’s veridical resolution, and recent synonymous-mapping semantic communication theory; and (iv) the Natural Possibility (NP) Framework, a data-driven possibilistic account that converts unimodal frequency data into natural possibility distributions via a modal conversion rule, and defines workable measures — Proximity Value (PV), Elemental Proximity Value (EPV), Mean Proximity Value (MPV), and a semantic measure SM — for precisiating vague human commands in machine reasoning. The article identifies a specific gap in the existing literature — the absence of an operational bridge linking uncertainty taxonomy, the LOA hierarchy, and computable possibilistic measures — and evaluates the extent to which the possibilistic account addresses it, alongside its limitations relative to contemporary coding-theoretic semantic communication frameworks. Open research directions in approximate reasoning, explainable AI, and 6G semantic communication are identified.

papers.title: NeuroShield IDS: AI-Powered Intrusion and Scam Detection System
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract Network intrusions and phishing attacks are growing problems for digital infrastructure. Spam messages and fraudulent legal notices add to the threat. Most Intrusion Detection Systems and spam filters still work separately, though. They also rely on static, rule-based logic. That does not hold up well against adaptive adversaries and new attack patterns. This paper presents NeuroShield IDS, an AI-powered system. It brings network intrusion detection and NLP-based scam/phishing classification into one place. Random Forest handles network-threat classification on the NSL-KDD and CICIDS2017 datasets. Naive Bayes with TF IDF vectorization handles scam and phishing detection on the SMS Spam Collection Dataset. A unified risk-scoring engine combines the severity signals from both modules. It sends real-time alerts through a Flask/Streamlit dashboard. Our experiments show over 97% accuracy for network intrusion detection. Scam classification stays above 95%. F1-scores hold up strong across every threat category. Keywords—Intrusion Detection System (IDS); Machine Learning; Random Forest; Naive Bayes; TF-IDF; Natural Language Processing (NLP); Phishing Detection; Cybersecurity; NSL-KDD; CICIDS2017; Risk Scoring

papers.title: A Distilbert Case-Based Deep Learning Model for Part-of-Speech Tagging for Under-Resourced Kenyan Language: A Case of Dholuo
papers.venue: International Journal of Computer Trends and Technology
papers.abstract: One of the basic Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks is Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging, which helps in various applications like sentiment analysis and information retrieval. However, creating accurate POS taggers for low-resource African languages continues to be difficult due to the scarcity of linguistic resources that are annotated. Its contribution is a deep learning method for POS tagging of Dholuo, a less-resourced Western Nilotic language, spoken by about four million people in Kenya and Tanzania. The suggested system uses DistilBERT, a small transformer model, in addition to FastText and Word2Vec vector representations of words that are used to capture the context and meaning of a word. The KenCorpus Dholuo POS dataset was carefully preprocessed, normalized, and standardized with the Universal POS tags and balanced using a hybrid resampling strategy to bring about class representation. The proposed method combines contextual transformer representations with complementary word representations and a training strategy that is optimized for the linguistic features of Dholuo, while previous studies primarily used multilingual transformer models or traditional sequence-labeling methods. The framework developed is a computationally efficient one that is well-suited for low-resource language processing. The results of the experiments reveal that the proposed DistilBERT-based model outperforms the baseline Conditional Random Field (CRF) and Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) models with an accuracy 79.05%, precision 80.63%, recall 79.05% and F1-score 79.24%. To our best knowledge, these results are the best reported for Dholuo POS tagging, and for under-resourced languages in Africa in general, highlighting the suitability of lightweight transformer architectures.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence tools for automating assessments of reporting guideline adherence: a protocol for a systematic review
papers.venue: F1000Research
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
papers.abstract: Background Complete reporting of health-related research is necessary for users to understand, appraise, and apply research results appropriately. Reporting guidelines have been developed to support complete reporting. However, assessments of reporting guideline adherence remain inconsistent, time-consuming, and difficult to scale. Artificial intelligence (AI) tools, such as traditional natural language processing models and large language models, might provide a potential solution. While numerous AI tools have been developed, no comprehensive synthesis has been undertaken to investigate what they assess, how they are implemented and perform, and their potential utility. Objective This systematic review aims to synthesise the characteristics and findings of studies evaluating AI tools developed to assist or automate assessments of reporting guideline adherence. Methods We will search MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Europe PMC, ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, arXiv and Cochrane Colloquium Abstracts, with no restrictions on date, language, or publication type. We will include studies that evaluate AI tools to assess adherence of health-related papers to any reporting guidelines. Two authors will independently screen records, extract data and assess risk of bias. We will extract study characteristics, AI tool details, how reporting guidelines are operationalised for AI assessment, AI implementation details, comparison details, and evaluation outcomes including agreement metrics, classification performance metrics, utility indicators, and tool reliability. We will present and summarise results through structured tables and plots, stratified by reporting guideline and AI tool type. Discussion This systematic review will provide a comprehensive synthesis of AI tools developed to automate assessments of reporting guideline adherence. It will provide interest holders with insights into what AI tools have been used, their implementation approaches, which AI tool types perform well, and any improvements that can be made to AI tools automating assessments of reporting guideline adherence in the future.

papers.title: A semi-automated LLM-based framework for word sense disambiguation in Serbian
papers.venue: Intelligent Data Analysis
papers.abstract: Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) remains a challenge in natural language processing, particularly for morphologically rich and less-resourced languages, e.g., Serbian, where complex inflectional systems intensify lexical ambiguity. Existing WSD approaches often struggle because of scarce annotated corpora, inadequate sense inventories, and linguistically complex languages. This paper presents a semi-automated framework for Serbian WSD resource development that employs Large Language Models (LLMs) and a constrained JSON-formatted output. The approach combines LLM-assisted sense assignment with a Serbian WordNet-based custom inventory, iterative inventory expansion, and expert validation, with the aim of supporting the practical construction and refinement of sense-annotated resources in a low-resource setting. In WSD experiments, LLMs significantly outperformed the Serbian-specific TeslaXLM , the multilingual embedding model intfloat/multilingual-e5-large , and the sentence transformer all-MiniLM-L6-v2 . The expanded sense inventory improved the accuracy, particularly for GPT-4.1 , which achieved 92.4% for single-word and 95.2% for multi-word spans. These results position LLMs as potentially practical for scalable sense-annotated data creation in less-resourced settings. The proposed methodology addresses key limitations in existing WSD pipelines for Serbian, and contributes to the broader effort of adapting LLMs for semantic processing in linguistically diverse and data-scarce environments.

papers.title: COMMUNITY SERVICE: Socialization and Distribution of Illustrated Dictionary of Medicinal Plants Product to the Community and Schools in Sabu Raijua
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Revitalization and preservation of biodiversity, particularly local plant species, is one of the key issues in sustainable development. The region of East Nusa Tenggara, especially areas like Sabu Regency, is known for its rich endemic flora. Local plants are not only part of the natural ecosystem but are also closely tied to the cultural identity, history, and daily life of the Sabu Raijua community. However, the phenomena of globalization, urbanization, and low environmental awareness have led to many local plant species becoming endangered due to land conversion, overexploitation, and the loss of traditional local knowledge passed down through generations (Bawono, 2019; Khairina et al., 2020; Matheus, 2020). This community service activity arises from an awareness of the existing problems or gaps in the field, such as the lack of public understanding especially among the younger generation, regarding the importance of local plants. In addition, many schoolchildren no longer recognize local plant species, whether in terms of their ecological benefits, traditional uses, or cultural values. Another aspect that underscores the need for this activity is the lack of educational media, such as illustrated dictionaries based on local plants, which could help introduce these plants in an engaging, visual, and easily understandable way for children (Markhamah et al., 2021; Hanafi et al., 2024; Latamada & Moussadecq, 2024). Moreover, outreach programs on the conservation of local plants are often neglected. In relation to the above issues, questions arise regarding the scientific relevance and positive impact of this community service activity. This program is designed not only as a form of practical service but also as a means of applying scientific knowledge in the fields of conservation biology, ethnobotany, environmental education, and science communication (Gunarso, 2021). Through an approach that combines outreach activities and the distribution of illustrated dictionaries, community-based conservation can be strengthened, as the community will be engaged as the main actors in preservation efforts, not merely as passive recipients. Furthermore, the use of visual media such as illustrated dictionaries supports the theory of multimodal learning, which suggests that children learn more effectively through a combination of text and images. From the perspective of community contribution, the outcomes of this activity are expected to enhance public awareness and understanding of the importance of local plant conservation, provide long-term educational tools that can be used by schools and community groups, and stimulate the emergence of local initiatives, such as school gardens or local plant adoption programs. Meanwhile, from the scientific contribution side, this activity can generate preliminary data on community perceptions, knowledge levels, and the effectiveness of visual media in environmental education, which can later be developed further as material for future studies or research. According to Wang et al. (2023), outreach and the distribution of educational media designed contextually to meet local needs can serve as important catalysts in safeguarding the sustainability of natural heritage, building ecological awareness, and strengthening the cultural identity of the Sabu community.

papers.title: Data used in "Multi-omics integration and batch correction using a modality-agnostic deep learning framework"
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: These are multimodal dataset objects and trained model parameters used in the study. The files are organized in pairs, where each multimodal dataset (.h5mu file) corresponds to a trained model parameter file (.pt) generated using the MIMA (Multimodal Integration with Modality-agnostic Autoencoders) framework. Each .h5mu file stores multiple modalities along with their corresponding metadata and annotations, serving as input to the MIMA model. The .pt files contain the trained PyTorch model parameters obtained from training MIMA on the respective dataset. Contents VISIUM_MSI_Morphology_prostate_cancer.h5muMultimodal dataset combining spatial transcriptomics (Visium), mass spectrometry imaging (MSI), and histological morphology data from prostate cancer samples. Includes global and modality-specific metadata. mima_params_prostate_cancer.ptTrained MIMA model parameters corresponding to the prostate cancer dataset above. RNA_ATAC_ATAC5kbmerge.h5muMultimodal single-cell dataset integrating RNA expression and chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) data. There is a second ATAC modality representing the 5 kb merged peak matrix. Includes global and modality-specific metadata. mima_params_multiome5kbmerge.ptTrained MIMA model parameters corresponding to the RNA–ATAC5kbmerge multimodal dataset. scCITEseq.h5muSingle-cell CITE-seq dataset integrating RNA expression and surface protein measurements, with relevant cell- and modality-level metadata. mima_params_cite.ptTrained MIMA model parameters corresponding to the scCITE-seq dataset. File formats .h5mu: Multimodal data container (MuData format). .pt: PyTorch serialized model parameters.

papers.title: Towards Early and Accurate Disease Detection Through Multimodal Predictive Modeling: Fusion of Electronic Health Records, Medical Imaging, And Omics Data Using Interpretable Machine Learning.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Early detection of disease is a cornerstone for improving patient outcomes, reducing costs, and enabling preventative interventions. Traditional predictive models often rely on a single type of data (e.g., imaging, clinical labs, or genomics). However, human health is inherently multimodal, involving a variety of data sources such as electronic health records (EHRs), medical imaging, wearable sensor data, genomics, and clinical notes. Integrating these heterogeneous modalities into unified predictive modelsoffers a path to richer, more accurate, and more robust disease detection. In this paper, we present a comprehensive survey of methods in multimodal predictive modeling for early disease detection, illustrate architectural patterns and fusion strategies, discuss challenges (e.g. missing modalities, interpretability, generalizability, bias), and highlight promising directions. We also propose a reference architecture for developing such systems and suggest evaluation best practices.

Main Clean Code.ipynbPurposeMain Clean Code.ipynb is the primary research pipeline. It composes several interlocking workflows for:TabPFN-based embedding learning from clinical features with explicit NACCID traceability.Construction of five normalized pathology latent variables (0–1) via TabPFN imputation, correlation filtering, and SEM.DDPM-based conditional synthetic patient generation over the 5D pathology latent space (healthy → maximal pathology).Downstream prediction pipelines for ordinal and continuous neuropathology targets, including co-pathology and cost-group analyses, ROC/PR evaluation, and DDPM-augmented oversampling variants.11.1 TabPFN Embedding WorkflowThis section loads a NACC-style training CSV, performs standardized cleaning, and trains a TabPFN-based embedding model:Cleans custom missing codes (e.g. 8, 9, 88, 99, 888, 999, 88.8, 99.9) to NACCID, and lv columns, then fits a TabPFNEmbedding model on $X$ with target lvSUM.Saves:Embeddings as .npy (train_tabpfn_lvsum_embeddings.npy) and .csv with NACCID, lvSUM, and a sample_index column.Feature-name list and a small summary CSV with number of samples, features, device, and checkpoint paths.Throughout, the notebook enforces strict alignment between rows and NACCID and aborts if counts diverge.1This produces TabPFN embeddings that can be reused across downstream models while preserving sample-level traceability.1.2 Pathology Latent-Variable Module (SEM 0–1 Factors)The pathology latent module builds a 5D latent pathology representation scaled to:1Pathology feature extraction and imputationLoads neuropathology tables (e.g. Thal phase, CERAD, Braak stage, NIA–Reagan, TDP-43, Lewy body staging, infarcts, hemorrhages, vascular markers).Casts all selected pathology columns to numeric and imputes missing values column-wise using a TabPFN classifier trained on the other pathology features.1Correlation filtering / multicollinearity handlingUses absolute pairwise correlations to identify highly collinear measure groups (e.g. Braak stage vs BRAAKBScore) and keeps a single representative per group, logging which variables were kept and removed.1SEM latent-factor modelBuilds a SEM specification where each latent pathology factor (e.g. amyloid, tau/Braak/ADNC, needed.1Scaling to 0–1 and savingApplies a MinMax scaler to map factor scores to, where 0 ≈ low/no pathology and 1 ≈ maximal observed pathology.1Saves:LV1–LV5 columns plus NACCID as a dataframe.The scaling object (latent0to1_scaler.pkl) for later reuse.1These five normalized latent pathology factors are then merged with clinical tables and used as conditioning variables for DDPM sampling and for downstream modeling.1.3 DDPM-Based Synthetic Patient Generation (Latent 0–1)The DDPM section trains a conditional denoising diffusion model on TabPFN embeddings and latent pathology labels:TabPFN embedding with missingness masksConcatenates TabPFN probability embeddings with standardized missing-value masks for all clinical features.Stores the quantile transformer, mask scaler, and feature metadata in embedding_transformers.pkl to invert embeddings back to feature space.1DDPM architectureImplements a fully connected residual DDPM with:Time embedding (nn.Embedding+MLP), latent pathology embedding, and residual blocks with SiLU activations and LayerNorm.Diffusion schedule with 1000 steps and linear betas.1Training and generationTrains the DDPM on real training embeddings plus 5D latent pathology labels with cosine annealing LR for 300 epochs, saving model weights.Samples from the model for three canonical pathology settings:Healthy: all 0s in latent space (synthetichealthy0.csv).Moderate: all 0.5s (syntheticmoderate05.csv).Max pathology: all 1s (syntheticmaxpatho1.csv).Uses embedding_to_real_data to invert TabPFN probabilities and masks back to reconstructed feature space, assigning random values to masked entries as an approximate reconstruction step.1These synthetic cohorts are intended for distribution-shift analysis, DDPM-based oversampling, and qualitative exploration, not as direct replacement for real clinical data.1.4 Pathology Prediction PipelinesSeveral prediction workflows are implemented:Classical ML regression/classification per pathology groupLoads pathology targets and multiple clinical feature tables.For each pathology group (e.g. amyloid, tau/Braak/ADNC, TDP-43, Lewy, CVD), iterates over tables and targets, applying:Train/test splits (random or stratified for classification).Table-specific preprocessing with ColumnTransformer (median imputation for numeric features and one-hot encoding for categorical).Model fitting for Decision Trees, Random Forests, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost with optional grid search.Saves per-target models, metrics, and diagnostic plots into a nested output directory structure grouped by pathology, table, and model name.21Ordinal TabPFN + Random Forest ensemblesFor strictly ordinal targets, uses TabPFN-based classifiers combined with Random Forests in a VotingClassifier ensemble, with optional SMOTE or DDPM-based oversampling of rare classes.Computes comprehensive ordinal metrics: exact accuracy, ordinal MAE, weighted kappa, class-wise recall, and AUC for binary tasks.1Independent, leakage-robust pipelinesImplements stricter pipelines where each target is predicted from features only, with no other targets used as inputs, explicit train-only preprocessing, stratified splits, and explicit memory/CUDA cleanup after each target.21Co-pathology and cost-group analysesDefines cost groups over subsets of clinical tables (e.g. “low-cost clinical”, “imaging + biomarkers”) and evaluates pathology prediction across these groups.Provides post-processing scripts that aggregate per-target ROC/PR curves into micro/macro averaged ROC/PR summaries across experiments, and generates multi-panel plots comparing cost groups.21Outputs from these pipelines – including per-target metrics, feature-importance plots, and cost-group ROC/PR figures – are stored under the various pathology*results folders and bundled in CoPathologyModel&Result.zip.212. (e.g. 0/1, 1–3).Saves:A NACC-shaped ROSMAP clinical+pathology CSV with NACC-conformant columns.A mapping/review file documenting each ROSMAP source column, its NACC target, and any transformation logic applied.12.2 Munich Neurobiobank → NACC-style conversionThe Munich Neurobiobank section performs an analogous harmonization:Links Munich-specific clinical and pathology fields to NACC column names wherever possible.Converts free-text symptom and diagnosis descriptions into structured indicators using keyword rules and pattern matching.Implements proxy rules when multiple candidate variables map to the same NACC column, preferring the least-missing or clinically most specific source.Produces:A NACC-like CSV for the Munich Neurobiobank with standardized naming and coding.A mapping file summarizing source-to-target mappings and any proxy choices.12.3 Joint export with latent pathology factorsThe notebook also contains a companion workflow that merges:Harmonized clinical papers.title: Analyse en detectie van vroege reumatische hartziekte met behulp van goedkope ECG- en PCG-metingen door middel van machinaal leren
papers.venue: Lirias
papers.abstract: Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD) affects approximately 55 million people worldwide, with the Global South bearing the greatest burden, particularly among children, adolescents, and young adults. Recently, the WHO declared RHD a global health priority, targeting a 25% reduction in premature deaths by 2030. Achieving this goal requires cost‑effective and scalable interventions for early detection in at‑risk populations. However, in low-resource settings, effective RHD prevention is hindered primarily by the absence of periodic community-based screening programs. As a result, patients often present late with severe complications, overwhelming cardiology services and making valve surgery unaffordable or inaccessible for most. One potential solution is the use of machine learning methods applied to electrocardiogram (ECG) and phonocardiogram (PCG) recordings from low-cost, portable devices as a screening tool. This research investigates whether portable ECG and PCG devices can serve as an effective, low-cost screening modality for early, asymptomatic RHD in resource‑constrained settings. To design and validate a scalable, AI‑enabled screening framework using such low-cost devices, we first established a novel, comprehensive multimodal dataset consisting of ECG, PCG, and echocardiography recordings from 627 schoolchildren in high‑risk communities. Statistical analysis identified ECG biomarkers associated with early RHD, including PR interval (p<0.001), Pw/PR ratio (p<0.001), and P‑wave dispersion (p=0.008), demonstrating significant electrophysiological differences between asymptomatic RHD cases and healthy individuals. Furthermore, an automated ECG analysis pipeline using efficient heuristic waveform delineation algorithms was validated against deep learning models and manual PQRST annotations, achieving onset delineation errors of 11.9 ms (P-wave), 9.8 ms (QRS complex), and 17.0 ms (T-wave), with corresponding offset errors of 11.3 ms, 7.5 ms, and 13.2 ms, respectively. These results demonstrated comparable performance to deep learning approaches thereby feasible for real-time implementation that can be operated by local healthcare staff. Machine learning models trained on automate ECG‑derived temporal, time‑frequency, wavelet, and graph‑based features achieved an F1‑score of 62.8%, sensitivity of 59.6%, and PPV of 66.7% for asymptomatic RHD detection, while maintaining detection of 51.1-65.7% of true RHD cases across clinically relevant operating thresholds. In contrast, PCG features alone achieved an F1‑score of only 22.3%, and combining ECG with PCG did not improve performance, confirming ECG as the most informative low‑cost screening modality in asymptomatic cohorts. The approach also demonstrated strong clinical utility for symptomatic RHD triage, achieving 93.6% sensitivity and 68.5% PPV using time-frequency ECG features, increasing to 97.2% sensitivity and 92.1% PPV when trained using attention‑based Inception‑Time convolutional neural networks (CNNs). In summary, this study demonstrated that affordable portable ECG and PCG devices, combined with machine learning, can serve as a practical first‑line screening tool without requiring specialist operators or echocardiography at the point of care. Rather than replacing echocardiography, the system identifies children who are highly likely to require confirmatory assessment, enabling more efficient allocation of scarce healthcare resources while reducing unnecessary referrals. Future implementation should focus on expanding training datasets, adopting the updated 2023 WHF diagnostic criteria, and integrating multimodal clinical data through foundation models to improve screening sensitivity. These advances would enable community health workers to perform large‑scale decentralized screening. Consequently, this supports early detection, timely antibiotic prophylaxis, and ultimately reduces the need for costly valve surgery in low‑resource settings.

papers.title: Collaboratief leren in de tolkenopleiding: naar een veelzijdig, gesitueerd, en sociaal-interactioneel begrip van tolkonderwijs
papers.venue: Lirias
papers.abstract: This dissertation investigates collaborative learning (CL) in interpreter training and seeks to develop a more integrated understanding of how it has been addressed, conceptualized, experienced, and enacted. Although collaborative practices such as group practice and peer feedback are common in interpreter education, they have often been discussed through fragmented local terms rather than examined as part of a broader and more coherent understanding of collaborative learning. As a result, the collaborative dimension of interpreter learning has remained insufficiently conceptualized and only partially explored in interpreting studies. To address this gap, the dissertation adopts a progressive multi-study design consisting of five interconnected studies. The first study is a review-based meta-study that maps how CL and related collaborative dimensions have been addressed in translation and interpreting research and identifies conceptual and empirical gaps. The second study is conceptual in nature and develops a theoretical account of CL in interpreter training through the lens of Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory (CCLT), showing that the value of CL is conditional rather than automatic. The third study is perception-oriented and examines how interpreting trainees and trainers understand, experience, and evaluate CL and related collaborative practices in interpreter training. The fourth and fifth studies draw on multimodal interactional data, including mobile eye-tracking, to investigate how CL becomes observable in situated peer-feedback interaction. Taken together, the dissertation shows that CL in interpreter training is best understood not as a single pedagogical technique, but as a multifaceted, situated, conditional, and social-interactional process. It spans multiple phases, including preparation, practice, and feedback; its value depends on contextual, individual, and interactional conditions; and it is realized through communication, cooperation, evaluation, negotiation, and shared regulation among learners. The dissertation further demonstrates that feedback constitutes a particularly revealing site for examining collaborative learning in action, as it makes visible such processes as explanation, proposal, uptake, correction, and attention coordination. The dissertation makes conceptual, methodological, and pedagogical contributions. Conceptually, it establishes CL in interpreter training as a more coherent object of inquiry and brings CCLT into dialogue with interpreter-training research. Methodologically, it demonstrates the value of a progressive multi-study design and of combining mobile eye-tracking with sequential and multimodal analysis in interpreter-training interaction. Pedagogically, it suggests that CL should not be treated as a self-explanatory practice, but requires clearer framing, stronger scaffolding, and more explicit attention to the development of collaborative competence alongside interpreting competence.

papers.title: A Multimodal IoT Framework for Analyzing Student stress through Personalized Yoga Intervention and Explainable AI (XAI)
papers.venue: International Journal of Technology & Emerging Research
papers.abstract: Psychological stress among students is a critical public health issue, it affects academic performance and long-term mental stability. Traditional diagnostic methods like interviews and periodic counselling, which failed to provide continuous and personalized monitoring. This proposal introduces an automated framework Internet of Things (IoT) wearables and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to monitor physiological stress- to detect student stress in real time. The framework employs machine learning and deep learning models for multimodal stress prediction. It recommends personalized yoga interventions based on individual stress profiles. To address the "black box" nature of current deep learning architectures, we incorporate Explainable AI (XAI) techniques like SHAP and LIME. These used to ensure clinical transparency and user trust. This enables students and healthcare professionals to understand the factors influencing stress. The system is expected to enhance early stress detection, improve effectiveness, support decision making by healthcare professionals, and also encourage student engagement in preventive wellness practice. Performance may be evaluated using Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score, Mean Absolute Error and Explainability Score. In addition, the system sets off a personalized yoga recommendation engine that maps detected autonomic states to evidence-based asanas from the Common Yoga Protocol (CYP) to effectively restore emotional wellness. The proposed system aims to resolve the stress and provide personalized behavioral recovery to enhance student well-being. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence (AI); Internet of Things (IoT); Wearable Sensors; Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI); Student Stress Detection; Personalized Yoga Intervention

papers.title: The Effects of Different Approaches to Teaching Chinese Orthography on Character Acquisition and Reading Performance in Learners of Chinese as a Foreign Language: A Systematic Review
papers.venue: Research Synthesis in Applied Linguistics
papers.abstract: There is growing evidence investigating the effects of different instructional methods on character acquisition and reading performance in contexts where students are learning Chinese as a foreign language (CFL). However, efforts to present a comprehensive and transparent synthesis of the literature have been limited, with previous systematic reviews suffering from incomplete reporting and the absence of risk of bias assessments. This makes it difficult to guide effective research and leaves educators unable to draw meaningful conclusions to inform sound teaching practice. Therefore, a critical evaluation of the current state of knowledge is needed, especially given the global expansion of Mandarin as the predominant variety taught in educational settings, and the inherent challenges associated with learning Chinese orthography. A systematic search process identified 30 eligible studies, published between 1990-2024. Findings revealed five broad categories of pedagogical approaches: computer-assisted language learning, conventional (or traditional) techniques, holistic approaches (combining reading, writing, listening, speaking), timing of character teaching, and various presentation methods when introducing unfamiliar characters. Compared to conventional strategies like rote memorisation, studies generally favoured technology-enhanced or multimodal methods, holistic approaches, and different ways of presenting target items. Research on the timing of orthographic instruction was mixed, with some evidence promoting immediate teaching of characters over a pinyin-first approach. However, trustworthiness ratings indicated that the overall strength of the literature was generally weak, with 23 studies classified as having high risk of bias. The actual or potential effects of each approach, considered alongside its study quality, are crucial factors for CFL practitioners when deciding whether to maintain existing teaching strategies in the classroom or adopt those found in this review. Some instructional methods may be successful in certain learning contexts, but the overall low methodological quality of the available evidence makes it problematic to draw clear causal inferences and offer confident pedagogical recommendations. Future research must employ more robust and transparent study designs to support the development of evidence-informed CFL teaching.

papers.title: Transforming medical ethics education: a scoping review of experiential, digital, and AI-integrated pedagogies
papers.venue: BMC Medical Ethics
papers.abstract: Medical ethics education plays a central role in preparing health professionals for complex clinical decision-making. However, rapid technological advances, evolving healthcare systems, and increasingly intricate ethical dilemmas have highlighted potential limitations of relying exclusively on traditional lecture-based approaches.In response, a wide range of innovative educational strategies has emerged, yet a comprehensive overview of these approaches remains limited. This scoping review aimed to map and synthesize recent innovations in medical ethics education, identify their educational outcomes, and highlight key challenges and emerging trends across health professions education. A scoping review was conducted in accordance with established methodological frameworks and the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar were searched for English-language publications from January 2022 to March 2025. Two reviewers independently conducted the searches, screened titles and abstracts, assessed full-text reports, and charted data using predefined eligibility criteria and a standardized data-charting form. Disagreements at any stage were resolved through discussion; when consensus could not be reached, a third reviewer was consulted. Forty studies were included and synthesized descriptively using narrative and thematic analysis. The 40 included studies covered undergraduate, postgraduate, and continuing education across multiple health professions. The reported innovations were organized into four interconnected domains: (1) learner-centered pedagogical strategies, including experiential, case-based, problem-based, game-based, and discussion-based learning; (2) technology-enhanced approaches, including immersive technologies, digital platforms, mobile learning, and AI-related curricula; (3) reflective and authentic assessment approaches, including portfolios and project-based or multimodal assessments; and (4) implementation enablers, particularly faculty development, institutional support, and protected curricular time. Across the included literature, authors reported outcomes related to ethical sensitivity, moral reasoning, learner engagement, reflective capacity, and preparedness for digital and AI-related ethical challenges. Recent literature indicates growing interest in experiential, reflective, context-sensitive, and technology-supported approaches to medical ethics education. The included studies reported potentially beneficial educational outcomes; however, heterogeneity in study designs, settings, learner populations, and outcome measures, together with the absence of formal quality appraisal, limits conclusions about comparative effectiveness and causal impact. Faculty development, institutional support, and longitudinal curricular integration emerged as relevant implementation considerations. Further research using validated measures, longer follow-up, and appropriately controlled designs is needed to clarify which approaches may be beneficial, for whom, and in which contexts. The review protocol was registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF; DOI: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/UQSJC ).

papers.title: Multimodal transformer-enhanced deep learning for accurate assessment of mandibular third molar–inferior alveolar canal contact using panoramic radiography and CBCT slices
papers.venue: BMC Oral Health
papers.abstract: Accurate preoperative assessment of the spatial relationship between mandibular third molars (M3Ms) and the inferior alveolar canal (IAC) is essential to minimize the risk of nerve injury. While panoramic radiographs (PRs) are routinely used as a first-line modality, their two-dimensional nature limits diagnostic reliability, often necessitating confirmatory cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT). We developed a dual-stream, transformer-enhanced multimodal (panoramic radiography + selected CBCT slices) deep learning framework designed as a clinician-in-the-loop system. The model jointly processes paired panoramic radiographs and operator-selected CBCT slices to simulate a realistic specialist consultation. Four widely used high-performance backbones (ConvNeXt, Swin Transformer, ResNet-50, and VGG16) were systematically evaluated on a dataset of 250 paired PR–CBCT cases. Model performance was assessed using F 1 -score, precision, recall, and area under the ROC curve (AUC). Model interpretability was explored using SHAP-based explainability analysis. Among the evaluated architectures, the ConvNeXt-based model achieved the highest overall performance, with a macro F 1 -score of 0.9478, precision of 0.9515, and recall of 0.9468. The learned embeddings showed good class separability, and explainability analyses highlighted anatomically meaningful regions consistent with established radiographic risk signs. The proposed multimodal 2D framework demonstrates competitive and robust classification performance. By integrating expert slice selection with automated feature extraction, the model functions as a standardized decision-support tool, aimed at reducing diagnostic variability in complex boundary cases where visual interpretation alone may be subjective.
